Split Old Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Split, Croatia

Not demolished. Split's Jewish presence dates to Roman times: Jewish graves from the 1st to 3rd centuries CE have been found in this, the city's old cemetery, including one tombstone commemorating a Jew originally from Tiberias. In the 16th century, Sephardic Jews fleeing Spain and Portugal settled in Split; among the community's noted rabbis were three members of the Mussafia family, who served in the 19th century. In 1573, the city granted Mount Marjan to the Jewish community for use as a cemetery, and it remained in use for 400 years. During WWII, Nazis burned the cemetery's archive, including the original 1573 document granting its use; most of the city's Jews were exterminated, though some children were evacuated to Nonantola in Italy and later to British Mandate Palestine. The cemetery holds about 700 tombstones, the oldest dated 1717 (or 1861, according to other sources — a discrepancy the record itself notes), with inscriptions in Spanish, Italian, Croatian, and Hebrew reflecting the community's Sephardic origins. Two 17th-century tombstones brought from the islands of Hvar and Brač carry rare figurative decoration — one a dove with an olive branch, the other an angel ascending a ladder to heaven, with an epitaph describing the soul's rest in the Garden of Eden. The cemetery's chapel is now used as a coffee house, and in 2014 some graves were seriously vandalized; the site was added to Croatia's state list of national heritage in 1966.
